description: Hi we're team GOATS! We are two students from Enloe Magnet High School. We developed Quorum, a platform that can help monitor astronaut health during space missions.
summary:
Quorum is a health check-in for astronauts on long missions that also checks whether its own lab readings can be trusted. On Mars, a sick astronaut and a bad reading can look the same, Earth is up to 22 minutes away, and the samples used to verify a blood analyzer expire within months.

Quorum tracks heart rate, blood pressure, blood sugar, temperature, sleep and mood against each astronaut's own normal, and explains what to do next in plain language. Before a lab result is used, it checks whether the change is in one person, in something the whole crew shares, or in the measurement itself.

We tested this on NASA's real Inspiration4 bloodwork, where it turned four alarms into one retake, and on 2,000 simulated crews per scenario. We also report how often it is wrong.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Quorum is a daily health check-in for astronauts that also checks whether the lab results they rely on can be trusted.

Each astronaut completes a short daily check-in covering vital signs, sleep, mood, and a three-minute reaction-time test. Quorum compares each reading with that astronaut’s own baseline rather than a population average. Results appear on a clickable body map, with color-coded status indicators and instructions explaining how to take each measurement.

The Decide screen brings everything together into a Go / No-go recommendation for activities like spacewalks. It also shows exactly why Quorum reached that decision, so the crew can understand what changed and what needs attention.

THE IDEA BEHIND IT

Most health apps assume their measurements are correct. On Earth, that’s usually a reasonable assumption because laboratories can run control samples whenever needed. On a Mars mission, that’s not so simple. Control samples expire within months, while the mission lasts years.

We started asking a different question: when a blood result changes, how do we know whether the astronaut changed or the machine did?

Quorum looks for three patterns:

  • If one person’s results change while everyone else’s remain stable, it flags a possible individual health issue for the crew medical officer.
  • If the entire crew changes in a similar way, along with related markers, it looks for something they share, such as air, water, or food.
  • If everyone changes on just one test, it suspects the analyzer and asks for a retake before requesting a control sample.

There is one exception. If a reading crosses a critical threshold, the crew acts immediately, even if the measurement might be unreliable.

The idea comes from patient-based quality control, which hospitals already use to catch laboratory equipment problems by looking at patterns in patient results. We wanted to see whether the same idea could work for a crew of four on a long-duration mission.

HOW WE TESTED IT

We didn’t want to build something that simply looked convincing. We wanted to see whether the underlying approach actually worked.

1. Real astronaut data

We tested Quorum on NASA’s published Inspiration4 bloodwork: four crew members, 36 routine markers, and seven collection periods. We used the original measurements without changing them.

The day after landing, red-cell size dropped across all four crew members. However, every result was still within the laboratory’s normal range.

A system looking only at individual baselines could have raised four separate alarms. Quorum noticed that the crew members had already been drifting together before flight and that no related marker had moved. It therefore suspected the analyzer and requested one retake instead.

At the 45-day collection, Quorum also picked up elevated potassium and reduced glucose in three crew members’ samples, a pattern associated with blood samples that sat too long before processing.

2. Simulated faults

Next, we built 2,000 simulated crews per scenario using the real preflight measurements. We deliberately introduced known problems and measured how often Quorum caught them.

Some results:

  • It detected a 5% analyzer error in 98.6% of simulations.
  • When that error appeared again in the following collection, it correctly identified the analyzer as the likely cause in 73% of cases.
  • It correctly identified delayed samples in 88.5% of detected cases.
  • It correctly identified shared environmental causes in 91% of detected cases.

One thing we noticed was that Quorum often couldn’t identify the exact cause after just one abnormal collection. Rather than guessing, it would sometimes return “cause unclear” and wait for another reading. We considered that an important part of the design.

3. Making the results reproducible

We also wrote an automated test that recalculates every number on our Evidence page directly from NASA’s original files. Anyone can run the script and check our calculations.

4. Checking against another laboratory

This was particularly important because NASA’s public data doesn’t tell us what actually caused each unusual result.

The same blood samples were also analyzed by two other laboratories that measured 283 proteins. We used this separate dataset to see whether Quorum’s decisions agreed with biological evidence it had never seen.

One protein we looked at was interleukin-8 (IL-8), which is released by blood cells when samples sit unprocessed. Its levels increased in exactly the three samples Quorum flagged as delayed and decreased in the one sample it cleared.

We also compared the variation in our crew’s measurements against published values for healthy adults. For 16 of 17 markers, the crew’s day-to-day variation was at least as wide as the published values. This gave us some reassurance that we weren’t setting individual baselines too narrowly.

WHAT DIDN’T WORK

Quorum isn’t perfect, and we don’t want to hide that.

Even when nothing is wrong, about one in three draws still triggers a false crew-wide alarm on at least one marker.

In a stricter follow-up test, Quorum sometimes confused an analyzer error with a shared environmental cause. It also usually caught a delayed sample affecting just one astronaut but rarely identified the correct cause.

These are important limitations. Quorum is designed to help the crew decide what to trust and what to retest, not to diagnose someone or automatically recommend treatment.

Our complete methodology, assumptions, validation code, results, and limitations are available at:

https://quorum-nasa.vercel.app/proof.html

WHO WOULD USE IT?

Astronauts would complete the daily check-ins. The crew medical officer would use Quorum to decide which results to trust and which ones need to be repeated. Flight surgeons on Earth could review the reasoning behind those decisions once communication becomes available.

We also think the idea could be useful outside spaceflight. Rural clinics, research ships, and polar stations all deal with the same basic problem: running medical tests without having immediate access to a larger laboratory.

HOW WE BUILT IT

Quorum is a web application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and hosted on Vercel.

It can be installed on a device and works fully offline. It can read HL7 laboratory messages and Apple Health exports, and it connects to NASA’s DONKI API for live space-weather alerts when internet access is available.

The analysis and validation tests run in JavaScript using Node.js. We also tested the application against WCAG 2.2 AA accessibility requirements, and it passed the automated check.

LIMITATIONS AND WHAT’S NEXT

Quorum is a prototype, not a medical device. Its classifications are educated guesses based on patterns in the data, not confirmed diagnoses. The public NASA dataset doesn’t provide verified explanations for every abnormal result.

Our independent laboratory comparison supports some of Quorum’s classifications, but it doesn’t prove them. It involves only four people, and the original records don’t confirm the cause of each change. Three baseline collections per astronaut are also not enough to establish a precise picture of their normal health.

The demo crew history is simulated and clearly labeled. The underlying Inspiration4 blood measurements are real.

Our next steps are to have medical professionals review the classification rules, test the application with new users, and explore a trial in an isolated research environment such as ESA’s Concordia Station in Antarctica.
